title: Worry: generalized worry, obsessions and health anxiety
about: Worry and obsessive-compulsive questions: what the worry is about (everyday matters, intrusive thoughts, illness or appearance), how it is handled (rituals, checking, reassurance), body symptoms versus fear of illness, and how belongings affect the home.

questions.text: What is the worry mostly about: many everyday matters (work, money, family, health), one kind of unwanted thought or image the client tries to push away, having a serious illness, or how part of the face or body looks?
questions.why: Worry that hops between ordinary topics fits generalized anxiety. An unwanted, intrusive thought followed by an urge to neutralize it (washing, checking, praying a set way, seeking reassurance) points toward OCD. A narrow, lasting focus on having a serious illness points toward health anxiety, and a focus on a perceived flaw in appearance toward body dysmorphic concerns.

options.label: An unwanted intrusive thought or image the client tries to cancel out
options.note: Ask about rituals and how much time they take; unwanted thoughts with rituals point toward OCD.

options.label: Mostly about having or getting a serious illness
options.note: Ask about body checking, symptom searching and reassurance seeking, and make sure a medical review has been offered.

options.label: Mostly about how part of the face or body looks
options.note: Ask about mirror checking, covering the area and cosmetic treatment, and how much of the day it takes.

questions.text: Once a worry starts, can the client set it aside, or does it keep running despite their efforts?
questions.why: Worry that feels hard to stop or steer away from is one of the key features of generalized anxiety, and it shapes the choice of worry-focused techniques.

questions.text: Does the client worry more than the situation calls for about several areas of life, on most days?
questions.why: Broad, excessive worry on most days is the other key feature of generalized anxiety. Worry limited to one topic, or that fits real current problems, points elsewhere.

options.label: No: worry is limited or fits real problems

questions.text: Does the client repeat actions or mental acts (washing, cleaning, checking, counting, seeking reassurance) to ease the distress, and do these take a lot of time or get in the way?
questions.why: Rituals that eat up a large part of the day or disrupt daily life, done to ease an unwanted thought, are central to OCD and guide treatment toward exposure and response prevention.

options.label: Yes: time-consuming or getting in the way
Some rituals, but brief and not disruptive

questions.text: Is the fear of <trigger> mainly during panic surges, or a steady fear of being or becoming seriously ill that shows up as body checking, searching symptoms online or asking for reassurance?
questions.why: Fear of dying or of a heart attack that flares during attacks fits panic. A steady preoccupation with illness, with reassurance helping only briefly, points toward health anxiety.

options.label: A lasting preoccupation with illness
options.note: Ask about checking, searching and reassurance, and make sure a medical review has been offered.

questions.text: Is the main problem body symptoms that are clearly there and take over daily life, or fear of having an illness while body symptoms are few or mild?
questions.why: Persistent body symptoms that crowd out daily life point toward a somatic symptom pattern; the distress is real whether or not a medical cause is found. A fear of illness that normal results do not settle, with few symptoms, points toward health anxiety.

options.label: Body symptoms that are clearly there and take over daily life
options.note: Make sure a medical review has been done or is planned, and keep working with it rather than around it.

options.label: Fear of having or getting an illness, with few or mild symptoms

questions.text: What does the client do about the health worry?
questions.why: Checking the body, searching symptoms and asking for tests ease the worry for a moment and keep it going; staying away from doctors out of dread is the same habit turned around. Knowing which one is in play shapes the plan.

options.label: Checks the body, searches symptoms online or asks for tests or reassurance often
Stays away from doctors, test results or anything about illness

questions.text: What does the client do about the part of their looks that worries them?
questions.why: Mirror checking or avoiding, long grooming, covering the area, comparing, asking others and repeated cosmetic treatment are the habits that keep appearance worry going. They also separate it from social anxiety, where the fear is about being judged in general.

options.label: Checks or avoids mirrors, grooms for long stretches or covers the area
Keeps seeking cosmetic, skin or surgical treatment for it
Asks others again and again whether it looks all right

questions.text: How do belongings affect the home?
questions.why: When parting with things is very hard, what matters next is whether the main rooms can still be used and whether the clutter creates hazards. Safety at home (exits, fire, falls, pests) comes before any sorting plan.

options.label: The main rooms can no longer be used as meant (cooking, sleeping, sitting)
Blocked exits, fire or fall hazards, pests or unsanitary rooms
options.note: Plan for home safety first; with the client's consent, fire-safety or housing services can help.

options.label: Keeps buying or collecting free things beyond the space or need
